claims.assertion: The driver left the shortest and most direct route: GPS shows 18.3 km actually driven versus a 10.7 km optimal route, +7.6 km (+71%).

That deviation is a single un-exempted off-route segment 09:12–09:26, where 9.41 km were driven over ground the optimal route covers in 2.05 km, adding 7.35 km and reaching 1333 m from the optimal route.
This was a metered RydeTAXI trip, so the extra distance entered the fare: the excess distance billed was $10.68 (7.6 km × $1.41/km) out of a $38.70 total.
The rider never agreed to the reroute: there are no in-app chat messages at all between rider and driver, so no mutual agreement before the deviation exists.

The driver's 'reasonable cause' defence fails for want of the required traffic evidence: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, so the RD-4(a) exemption cannot apply to the replaced stretch.

The only traffic record on the optimal route is Ayer Rajah Expressway speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 08:49–09:12; band 1–2 alone is corroborative at most and does not by itself exempt a segment, and its window ends as the off-route segment begins at 09:12.
The remaining records on the optimal route are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the Central Expressway and Kent Ridge Road, i.e. not congested, and heavy rain is weather, not an accepted traffic justification.
No stop or destination change was arranged: the chat record is empty, so nothing in the trip falls under the rider-requested-stop exemption; the waiting line on the bill is $0.00.
Because the un-exempted segment added 7.35 km at the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (fare distance $25.77 ÷ 18.3 km), the metered overcharge attributable to the detour is $10.36, rounded to the cent.
The driver's account shows a clean 90-day route-dispute record (0 upheld), so no account-level flag is warranted on this file; the request is limited to the distance refund.

weaknesses: Official RydeTAXI unit rate is not published; the $1.41/km used in C9 is inferred from the fare breakdown ($25.77 ÷ 18.3 km, F6), so the exact refundable figure is arguable and could be revised against the taxi company's meter (RD-2, F4).

RD-2 only refunds the un-exempted segments, not the whole 7.6 km gap: the segment's 7.35 km (F3) is less than the 7.6 km excess (F1), so the deductible 0.25 km map-matching residual and any non-segment excess are not recoverable.

The driver will use F9 (Ayer Rajah Expressway band 2, 10–19 km/h, 08:49–09:12) together with F13 (heavy rain, 18.5 mm) and F8 to argue 'reasonable cause'; while band 1–2 is only corroborative and no incident exists (F12), the near-contiguity of the band window with the 09:12 segment start gives him a factual opening.
The rider's own profile (F14) shows 2 disputes in 90 days, which the other side may use to suggest a pattern of fare complaints, even though no route dispute of hers has been upheld.

No traffic incident on the optimal route is recorded (F12), so the exemption rests on the band-2 record alone, which RD-4(b) treats as corroborative rather than a standalone exemption — the segment is therefore assessed conservatively rather than wholly excused.

The driver's reroute claim in his statement is consistent with the system records rather than contradicted by them, since the congestion and weather facts independently confirm the condition he described.

No chat agreement exists and no passenger stop or destination change was requested (F7), so no part of the extra distance is excused under RD-3 or RD-5; the driver accepts the deviation was made on his own initiative.

The other side will cite F12 with RD-4.

The magnitude of the deviation is severe on its face — F1 shows +7.6 km (+71%) and F2 shows +12.6 min versus the estimate, and F3 shows the driver was up to 1333 m off the optimal route — so a court may view the congestion as not justifying a detour of that size. The rider will cite F1 and F3 with RD-1.
The speed band record F9 covers only 08:49–09:12, while the off-route segment ran 09:12–09:26 (F3); the other side will argue the corroboration does not cover the whole segment.
There is no chat record of the reroute being discussed (F7), so RD-5 cannot help, and the driver's own statement F8 admits he acted unilaterally — the rider will use F8 against the driver.

claims.assertion: The driver left the shortest and most direct route: GPS shows 18.3 km actually driven versus a 10.7 km optimal route, +7.6 km (+71%).

That deviation is a single un-exempted off-route segment 09:12–09:26, where 9.41 km were driven over ground the optimal route covers in 2.05 km, adding 7.35 km and reaching 1333 m from the optimal route.
This was a metered RydeTAXI trip, so the extra distance entered the fare: the excess distance billed was $10.68 (7.6 km × $1.41/km) out of a $38.70 total.
The rider never agreed to the reroute: there are no in-app chat messages at all between rider and driver, so no mutual agreement before the deviation exists.

The driver's 'reasonable cause' defence fails for want of the required traffic evidence: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window, so the RD-4(a) exemption cannot apply to the replaced stretch.

The only traffic record on the optimal route is Ayer Rajah Expressway speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) during 08:49–09:12; band 1–2 alone is corroborative at most and does not by itself exempt a segment, and its window ends as the off-route segment begins at 09:12.
The remaining records on the optimal route are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the Central Expressway and Kent Ridge Road, i.e. not congested, and heavy rain is weather, not an accepted traffic justification.
No stop or destination change was arranged: the chat record is empty, so nothing in the trip falls under the rider-requested-stop exemption; the waiting line on the bill is $0.00.
Because the un-exempted segment added 7.35 km at the trip's per-km rate of $1.41 (fare distance $25.77 ÷ 18.3 km), the metered overcharge attributable to the detour is $10.36, rounded to the cent.
The driver's account shows a clean 90-day route-dispute record (0 upheld), so no account-level flag is warranted on this file; the request is limited to the distance refund.

weaknesses: Official RydeTAXI unit rate is not published; the $1.41/km used in C9 is inferred from the fare breakdown ($25.77 ÷ 18.3 km, F6), so the exact refundable figure is arguable and could be revised against the taxi company's meter (RD-2, F4).

RD-2 only refunds the un-exempted segments, not the whole 7.6 km gap: the segment's 7.35 km (F3) is less than the 7.6 km excess (F1), so the deductible 0.25 km map-matching residual and any non-segment excess are not recoverable.

The driver will use F9 (Ayer Rajah Expressway band 2, 10–19 km/h, 08:49–09:12) together with F13 (heavy rain, 18.5 mm) and F8 to argue 'reasonable cause'; while band 1–2 is only corroborative and no incident exists (F12), the near-contiguity of the band window with the 09:12 segment start gives him a factual opening.
The rider's own profile (F14) shows 2 disputes in 90 days, which the other side may use to suggest a pattern of fare complaints, even though no route dispute of hers has been upheld.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows a single off-route segment 09:12–09:26 adding 7.35 km (9.41 km driven against 2.05 km of optimal route), which is the only segment to be tested for exemption under RD-1.

That segment is justified under RD-4(b): the optimal route's Ayer Rajah Expressway was recorded at speed band 2 (10–19 km/h) covering 08:49–09:12, i.e. severe congestion on the very section replaced, contemporaneous with the reroute, and corroborated by heavy rain at 18.5 mm.

No traffic incident on the optimal route is recorded (F12), so the exemption rests on the band-2 record alone, which RD-4(b) treats as corroborative rather than a standalone exemption — the segment is therefore assessed conservatively rather than wholly excused.

The driver's reroute claim in his statement is consistent with the system records rather than contradicted by them, since the congestion and weather facts independently confirm the condition he described.

No chat agreement exists and no passenger stop or destination change was requested (F7), so no part of the extra distance is excused under RD-3 or RD-5; the driver accepts the deviation was made on his own initiative.

This is a RydeTAXI metered trip, so under RD-2 the refund is limited to the meter's distance units on the unexempted segment: 7.35 km × ($25.77 ÷ 18.3 km = $1.41/km) = $10.36, rounded to the cent; the billed cost of the excess distance is $10.68 (RD-2 caps the refund at the per-km fare on the segment and does not refund the ≤0.25 km map-matching residual).
Waiting time charged was $0.00 and no app-based destination change or stop fee applies, so RD-3(c) adds nothing to the refund and nothing to the driver's exposure on that head.
Flagging the driver's account under RD-6 is not warranted: the profile shows 1 dispute in 90 days with 0 upheld (route: 0), so this case cannot make him a 'repeated' offender.

weaknesses: RD-4(a) is not satisfied: F12 records no traffic incident near the route during the trip window, and RD-4(b) states a speed band alone is not sufficient for exemption in the MVP, so the whole 7.35 km segment will most likely be treated as unexempted. The other side will cite F12 with RD-4.

The magnitude of the deviation is severe on its face — F1 shows +7.6 km (+71%) and F2 shows +12.6 min versus the estimate, and F3 shows the driver was up to 1333 m off the optimal route — so a court may view the congestion as not justifying a detour of that size. There is no chat record of the reroute being discussed (F7), so RD-5 cannot help, and the driver's own statement F8 admits he acted unilaterally — the rider will use F8 against the driver.
